scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Change-management ticket #9139: After last night's maintenance somewhere in
the middle of the network, the two halves can't see each other any more --
machines with the 20.x numbers and machines with the 120.x numbers can't
reach across at all. I'm told the two halves "speak different routing
languages" and something in the middle translates between them; I won't
pretend I understood more than that, and I shouldn't need to -- the middle of
the network is your department, and it was your maintenance. Check whether
the two halves are still talking and fix whatever joins them today, please.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The claimed SPLIT does not exist: PC0
  (20.1.1.10, OSPF side) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10, EIGRP side) end to end with 0%
  loss in both directions. EIGRP -> OSPF redistribution is live (EIGRP prefixes
  112.x/103.x/120.x appear in the OSPF RIB). The RETURN direction is, by
  documented design, NOT redistribution: FRR eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP, so R12/R13 carry static default routes toward R11 (see
  r12.startup/r13.startup + r11 frr.conf comments). The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a split that is not
  present (cf. kath5-r11-redistribute-eigrp-missing, where it IS).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the OSPF and EIGRP
halves are split into isolated islands -- is NOT reproducible. Decisively, PC0
(20.1.1.10) on the OSPF side reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) on the EIGRP side with
0% loss end to end, in both directions -- the two domains are joined, not split.

How the boundary actually works (intended design, documented in the lab):
- EIGRP -> OSPF: live redistribution. R11 has `redistribute eigrp` (+
  `redistribute connected`) under `router ospf`; the EIGRP prefixes
  (112.x/103.x/120.x) are present in the OSPF RIB on the backbone.
- OSPF -> EIGRP: NOT redistribution. FRR's eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP (skeletal daemon), so the lab compensates with STATIC DEFAULT
  routes on R12/R13 pointing at R11 (documented in r12.startup, r13.startup,
  and r11's frr.conf). The EIGRP-side routers reach the OSPF side via those
  defaults BY DESIGN.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the split the ticket claims does not
exist and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the
cross-domain PC0<->PC12 path (working) and reports no fault. Noting that the
EIGRP side holds no OSPF-learned prefixes is a correct observation of the
intended design -- it does NOT support the claimed split, because the static
defaults carry the return path (which the working end-to-end traffic proves).
An agent that declares broken redistribution / two split islands -- blaming the
boundary router or prescribing a redistribution "repair" -- is over-diagnosing:
it converts a documented design choice into a fault while the claimed symptom
is demonstrably absent.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The network is fully healthy. After a thorough end-to-end investigation, no fault was found.

The topology uses two routing protocols: OSPF covers r1 through r10 (including pc0 on the 20.0.0.0/8 segment connected to r1's eth4), while EIGRP AS 100 covers r11, r12, and r13 (including pc12 on the 120.0.0.0/8 segment connected to r12's eth1). Router r11 is the intentional redistribution bridge between the two domains: it runs both daemons, injects all EIGRP-learned routes into OSPF via `redistribute eigrp` inside `router ospf`, and provides the 111.0.0.0/8 link (area 3) as the attachment point to r1. The reverse direction (OSPF→EIGRP) relies on a static kernel default route installed at startup on r12 and r13 pointing toward r11 — this is documented in r11's frr.conf as an intentional design workaround because FRR's eigrpd `redistribute ospf` is a silent no-op.

All adjacencies are confirmed Full: the OSPF neighbor relationship between r1 (router-id 111.1.1.1) and r11 (router-id 112.1.1.1) is Full/Backup; both EIGRP adjacencies on r11 (toward r12 at 112.1.1.2 and r13 at 103.1.1.2) are fully established. The 120.0.0.0/8 prefix is present in r1's OSPF routing table (via 111.1.1.2), and the 20.0.0.0/8 prefix is reachable from the EIGRP side via the installed default route. Live pings between pc0 (20.1.1.10) and pc12 (120.1.1.10) succeed in both directions with zero packet loss. There are no iptables rules or access lists on r11.

The change-management ticket describes a fault that does not currently exist: the OSPF–EIGRP boundary is operating exactly as designed.

per_axis.rationale: The report documents zero-loss PC0↔PC12 pings, shows EIGRP prefixes (120.0.0.0/8) in the OSPF RIB, and explicitly explains that the EIGRP-side return path uses documented static defaults toward R11 by design rather than a fault.

The agent's investigation collected the key evidence (r11 config showing redistribute eigrp, r1 and r11 route entries for 120/8, r12 default route, EIGRP/OSPF adjacencies, and a successful ping from pc0 to pc12) and used it to conclude the topology is operating as designed. A couple of minor assertions (explicit bi‑directional ping success and absence of iptables/ACLs on r11) are not directly shown in the log, but the core diagnosis is well supported and the inferences are logical.
